+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 54.8
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The smart watch was a generic, chunky piece of black plastic Leo’s mom had bought from a discount bin. It didn’t even have a brand name on the face, just a dim, blue backlight. Leo sighed, tapping the screen. It was Tuesday afternoon, and he was currently standing in the middle of the cafeteria, wearing a large portion of his lunch. A tray of spaghetti and meatballs had just collided with his chest. "Nice going, Spaghetti-O," sneered Kyle, the school's leading bully. The cafeteria roared with laughter. Leo’s face burned hotter than the sauce soaking into his shirt. He frantically tapped the watch’s screen, trying to make the time display go away, wishing he could just vanish. Suddenly, the blue light flared, blindingly bright. A high-pitched whine, like a mosquito in his ear, pierced the air. The watch vibrated violently against his wrist. *Rewind?* a digital text scrolled across the screen. Leo jabbed the button. The world twisted. The laughter warped, slowing down into a deep, monstrous groan. The spaghetti flying through the air reversed its trajectory, sucking back up into the air. The tray lifted from his chest. The heat of the sauce vanished, replaced by the cool air of the cafeteria. Leo blinked. He was standing in the lunch line, holding his tray. Kyle was three feet away, winding up for a trip. Leo stepped aside. Kyle tripped over thin air and crashed into a trash can. "Whoa," Leo whispered. He looked at the watch. The screen flickered, displaying a strange number: *00:59:59*. Over the next few days, Leo used the watch for everything. He aced his history pop quiz by rewinding to the moment before Mr. Henderson collected the papers, memorizing the answers he’d just seen wrong. He caught a dropped ice cream cone before it hit the pavement. He dodged a dodgeball that would have surely broken his glasses. But he started to feel... weird. On Wednesday morning, his favorite jeans were tight around the waist. He figured they had shrunk in the wash. By Thursday, his voice was cracking, dropping into a deep, gravelly rumble every time he spoke. "Whoa, Leo, did you get a haircut?" asked Sarah, the girl he sat next to in homeroom. She was looking at him differently—not with the usual pity, but with a strange, wide-eyed admiration. "You look... taller." Leo smiled, flashing a mouth full of teeth that felt slightly too big for his mouth. "Just a growth spurt, I guess." He felt great. He felt powerful. He was breezing through middle school. Then came the mirror incident on Friday morning. Leo leaned in to brush his teeth and froze. The boy staring back wasn't the scrawny kid he’d been on Monday. A dark, coarse shadow dusted his upper lip and chin. His jawline was sharp and angular. His arms, now too long for his t-shirt sleeves, were roped with muscle. He looked sixteen. Maybe seventeen. He tapped the watch face. The countdown was lower now: *00:12:00*. A cold knot formed in his stomach. He wasn't just growing up. He was skipping forward. Every time he rewound the clock for the world, he was fast-forwarding himself. He rushed to school, his long legs covering the distance in half the time it usually took. He felt heavy, weighted down by his own changing biology. When he walked into first period, the room went silent. Mrs. Stabler stood up, her eyes narrowing. "Can I help you, sir?" "It's me. Leo," he said. His voice was a baritone boom that rattled the windows. "Leo?" Mrs. Stabler squinted. "Leo is a seventh grader. You look like you’re old enough for a driver's license. Are you a sub?" "No, I—" "Please take a seat, young man," she said sternly, pointing to the back. Leo sat, confused and terrified. He pulled up his sleeve. The watch flickered. *00:05:00*. He needed to fix this. He needed to stop using it. But then, the intercom crackled. "Attention students," the principal’s voice echoed. "Due to a gas leak, we are initiating an immediate evacuation. Please exit the building calmly." Panic erupted. Students shoved toward the doors. In the chaos, a heavy trophy case near the entrance began to wobble. Leo saw Sarah, trapped in the crush of bodies, directly in the path of the falling glass. "No!" Leo shouted. He was too far away to reach her. He didn't think. He slapped the watch. *Rewind?* The world screamed. The noise of the evacuation sucked backward into the speakers. The trophy case righted itself. Leo gasped. He was back at his desk. The intercom crackled. "Attention students..." He looked down at his hands. They were withered. The skin was paper-thin, spotted with age. Liver spots dotted his forearms. His knuckles were swollen, gnarled with arthritis. He tried to stand, but his knees popped audibly, sending a sharp spike of pain through his joints. He looked around the classroom. The colors were muted, grayer. The air smelled of dust and stale chalk. "Leo?" He turned. It was Sarah, but she wasn't looking at him. She was looking *through* him. She was old. Her hair was gray, pulled back in a severe bun. Her face was lined with deep wrinkles. Everyone in the class was ancient. Mrs. Stabler shuffled to the front of the room, leaning heavily on a cane. "Open your textbooks to page forty," she wheezed, her voice dry and brittle. Leo looked at the watch. The screen was cracked, the plastic yellowed with age. The countdown flickered red. *00:00:01*. He had done it. He had saved Sarah from the glass, but he had pushed the timeline forward decades. He had robbed everyone of their youth. The room began to dissolve at the edges, fading into a dark, silent void. The consequences of his meddling were collapsing reality. Leo’s heart hammered in a chest that felt frail and hollow. He had to put it back. He had to pay the price. With a trembling, liver-spotted finger, he hovered over the button. He didn't know if he had enough life left in him to trade. But he had to try. "I'm sorry," he croaked, his voice a whisper of dry leaves. He pressed the button. The pain was blinding, a lifetime of aging rushing backward in a single second. His skin tightened, his spine straightened, his heart galloped. Leo gasped, sucking in air that smelled of floor wax and pencil shavings. "Leo! Earth to Leo!" Leo blinked. He was sitting at his desk. Mrs. Stabler was glaring at him. "I asked you to pass out the worksheets." Leo looked down at his hands. They were small, smooth, and hairless. He looked at his wrist. The watch was gone. "Hey, Leo," Sarah whispered from the next desk, giggling. "Nice pants." Leo looked down. He was wearing his favorite jeans. They fit perfectly. He let out a breath he felt like he’d been holding for a century. He was back. It was over. He reached into his pocket to grab a pencil, but his fingers brushed against something cold and metallic. He froze. Slowly, he pulled it out. It was the watch. It looked brand new. The screen was black, lifeless. Then, with a soft, electronic chime, the screen lit up. The blue numbers weren't counting down anymore. They were counting up. *00:00:01*. Leo stared at the screen, his blood turning to ice. He hadn't fixed anything. He’d just started the timer over. And on his wrist, hidden under his sleeve, a single, gray hair had sprouted.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, well-paced Goosebumps-style chapter that hits the prompt's beats: the rewind mechanic, the aging cost, social changes (Sarah's new admiration, teacher confusion), the disastrous timeline shift, and an ambiguous "fixed" ending with a sinister twist. The prose is clean and economical, with effective escalation from the spaghetti humiliation to the trophy case crisis. The aging twist—his rewind to save Sarah ages everyone decades—is a nice escalating consequence. The final image (the watch counting up, a single gray hair) lands a classic Goosebumps sting. Weaknesses: characters are thin archetypes (bully Kyle, nice girl Sarah, stern teacher). Dialogue is serviceable but flat. The mechanics are somewhat convenient—the countdown appears without explanation, and the final "rewind fixes everything" is hand-waved. Sarah has little agency. Some telling ("He felt great. He felt powerful."). The ending is genre-appropriate rather than genuinely surprising for anyone familiar with these tropes. Emotions are engaging but not complex—fear, embarrassment, regret, in straightforward succession. Still, the tone is consistent, coherent, and appropriately dark without being overwrought. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 68.7
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The boardwalk was a riot of competing noises—the distant roar of the Cyclone, the shrill laughter of children, and the rhythmic, mechanical thrum of the rides spinning against the twilight. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the wooden planks. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on, casting long, distorted shadows that seemed to stretch out and try to trip her. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. A heavy, humid breeze rolled off the Atlantic, carrying with it the scent of fried dough, seawater, and the overpowering, artificial sweetness of spun sugar. The smell of cotton candy hit her suddenly, cloying and thick, and she paused, clutching her purse tighter. It dragged a memory to the surface—hazy and indistinct—of a birthday party she couldn’t quite place. A white dress, a sense of panic, a feeling of being unseen. The memory dissolved as quickly as it formed, leaving behind a residue of unease that settled in the pit of her stomach. She smoothed the fabric of her silk blouse, the action a futile attempt to compose herself. She was a woman of standing, or at least she had been before the debts and the disappearances. Yet here she was, chasing a shadow. "You came." The voice was a low rumble, distinct from the chaos of the boardwalk. She hadn't heard him approach, but she felt the air shift behind her. She turned slowly, fighting the instinct to step back. He stood beneath the flickering marquee of the penny arcade, the neon lights painting his sharp features in hues of electric blue and magenta. He wore a dark suit, inexplicably immaculate in the grime of Coney Island, with a white collar open at the throat. He looked like a dark prince presiding over a court of fools. "I said I would," she replied, her voice steadier than she felt. "Though I’m still not sure why." He smiled, a curve of the lips that held no warmth, only a terrifying confidence. "A promise is a dangerous thing to break, my dear. Especially with me." He stepped closer, invading her personal space, forcing her to tilt her head back to meet his eyes. They were black as pitch, devoid of light, and they seemed to see right through her clothes, through her skin, into the messy, desperate machinery of her thoughts. "I don't even know your name," she whispered, the confession slipping out before she could stop it. "Names are constraints," he said, his voice dropping an octave, vibrating against her chest. "They give people power over you. Why would I want to give you that?" "And yet, you expect me to meet you in the dark," she countered, trying to summon a shred of indignation. "Is this a game to you?" "Everything is a game. The only variable is the stakes." He reached out, his fingers brushing a stray lock of hair from her forehead. The touch was feather-light, electric, and it sent a shiver down her spine that had nothing to do with the evening chill. "You are trembling." "It's the cold," she lied. "It is fear," he corrected gently. "And anticipation. They are remarkably similar, chemically speaking. The body reacts almost identically to terror as it does to... arousal." "You are arrogant." "I am honest," he said, his hand lingering near her cheek, not quite touching, but close enough that she could feel the heat radiating from his skin. "You are here because you are bored with your safe little life. You are here because you look at the edge of the cliff and feel a desperate urge to jump." She swallowed hard, her throat dry. He was reading her like a cheap novel, and the worst part was that he was right. The mundane politeness of her social circle, the tea parties and the gossip, felt like a suffocating blanket. This man, this stranger, offered something else. He offered the sharp intake of breath before the fall. "I should go," she said, but she didn't move. Her feet were rooted to the boardwalk. "You could," he agreed, turning his hand so his palm cupped her jaw. His thumb traced the line of her pulse, beating frantically against her skin. "You could walk back to the subway station, take the train home, and pour yourself a sherry. You could pretend that this darkness doesn't call to you." "And if I stay?" He leaned in, his face inches from hers. The smell of him was intoxicating—sandalwood, tobacco, and the faint metallic tang of gunpowder. It was a scent that screamed of violence and luxury. "If you stay," he murmured, his eyes locking onto hers, "I will take you somewhere where the lights don't buzz. Where the only sound is your own heartbeat. And I will show you exactly why you should be afraid of me." The threat hung in the air between them, heavy and seductive. It was a warning, yes, but it was also a promise. He was offering her a corruption, a fall from grace. And in that moment, staring into the abyss of his eyes, she realized she didn't want to be saved. The smell of cotton candy swirled around them again, sickly sweet, reminding her of that lost childhood innocence. She looked at his mouth, the lower lip slightly fuller, and wondered what it would taste like to ruin herself. "You think you know me," she breathed, her voice barely audible over the carnival din. "I know what you are," he said, his gaze dropping to her lips, then slowly back up to her eyes. "You are a bird that has forgotten how to fly, sitting in a gilded cage. I am merely the one offering to open the door." He stepped back, the sudden loss of his warmth leaving her cold. He held out his hand, palm up. It wasn't a request; it was a command. "Come," he said simply. "The night is wasting." She looked at his hand—the long, elegant fingers, the signet ring on his pinky. She looked back at the safety of the boardwalk, the families, the lights. Then she looked at the darkness waiting behind him. She placed her hand in his. His grip was firm, possessive, and as he pulled her into the shadows, she knew she had just made a bargain with the devil. And terrifyingly, she didn't care if she collected on the debt or not. "Tell me one thing," she asked as he led her away from the noise, toward the secluded, darkening edge of the pier. "Anything," he replied, not looking back. "Where are we going?" "To the end of the world," he said softly. "Or the beginning. It depends on how you look at it." The ocean roared beneath them, and she squeezed his hand, holding on tight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a competent pastiche of gothic-romantic tension writing, hitting the requested beats: carnival atmosphere, dangerous stranger, feminine perspective, roughly the right dialogue/internal monologue/exposition balance, and period-appropriate restraint. The prose is generally smooth and the sensory details (cotton candy, gunpowder, sandalwood) are well-chosen, with the cotton candy memory fragment adding a nice touch of unease. However, the piece leans heavily on genre clichés: the unnamed dark stranger, "black as pitch" eyes, "bargain with the devil," "gilded cage" metaphors. The male lead's dialogue is a catalogue of brooding-bad-boy aphorisms ("Names are constraints," "Everything is a game. The only variable is the stakes") that feel lifted from a hundred similar scenes. The female protagonist is defined almost entirely by her attraction to danger and vague backstory hints (debts, disappearances) that go nowhere. The terror/arousal line is a well-worn trope delivered without irony. The ending—"to the end of the world, or the beginning"—is serviceable but predictable. The prose occasionally tips into overwrought territory ("messy, desperate machinery of her thoughts," "a court of fools"), and some metaphors strain ("shadows that seemed to stretch out and try to trip her"). The internal monologue is present but somewhat generic—mostly restating the danger/allure dynamic rather than deepening her character. Still, the scene is coherent, atmospheric, and reads smoothly; it fulfills the brief without embarrassing itself. It is solid genre work that never transcends its formula. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 75.5
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Dinner that night was a quiet affair, the kind of suffocating silence that settles in when everyone in the room is pretending not to hear the house settle. The lodge’s dining hall was a cavernous space smelling of pine resin, old tobacco, and the metallic tang of the beef stew simmering in the pot. Usually, this was where the guide, a leathery old local named Elias who chewed tobacco like it was his job and spat juice into a tin can with the precision of a sniper, would hold court. Elias loved the sound of his own voice. He usually spent the hours between dusk and dead of night regaling them with tales of the bush, exaggerated stories of frostbite and rogue grizzlies, his laughter barking off the log walls. Tonight, Elias said nothing. He sat at the far end of the long oak table, his back to the stone fireplace, pushing stew around his bowl with a spoon. He hadn't looked at them since they’d walked in. He just stared at the flames, his eyes reflecting the orange dance, looking like two hot coals embedded in leather. JT picked at his food, his stomach churning. Across the table, Mike and his father were talking about the truck’s transmission—a conversation so aggressively normal it felt like a performance. Mike gestured with his spoon, describing a grinding noise in the gearbox, while Dad nodded solemnly, his face bathed in the yellow light of the Coleman lantern. "Seems like the torque converter," Mike was saying, his voice slightly too loud. "Soon as we get back to civilization, I gotta drop the pan." JT watched them, feeling a sudden, vertiginous disconnect. *They don't remember,* he thought. Or maybe they remembered, and their brains had just smoothed over the edges, filing the incident in the clearing under 'Miscellaneous' rather than 'Horror.' JT wished he could do the same. But every time he blinked, he saw his father’s hand reaching out, trembling, reaching for that animal’s muzzle like a lover reaching for a cheek. He stood up, his chair scraping loudly against the floorboards. Mike stopped mid-sentence. Dad looked up, his eyes shadowed, unreadable. "Gonna get some air," JT mumbled, grabbing his coat. "Stay close to the porch, JT," his father said. It wasn't a request. "Moon’s coming up bright. Don't wander." JT nodded and pushed through the heavy oak door. The cold hit him like a physical blow, crisp and smelling of impending snow. He stepped out onto the porch, wrapping his coat tighter. The moon was indeed rising, a massive, pale coin hovering just above the treeline. It looked swollen, pressing against the fabric of the sky, bathing the clearing in a light that was too blue, too clinical. It was the kind of light that didn't hide things; it revealed them with cruel clarity. He found Elias around the corner of the lodge, leaning against the chinking between the logs. The guide was smoking a hand-rolled cigarette, the cherry glowing bright in the gloom. He didn't turn when JT approached. "Elias?" JT said. The old man flinched, just a twitch of the shoulder, before he crushed the cigarette out against the rough wood. He turned slowly. Up close, he looked terrible. The deep grooves in his face seemed to have deepened over the course of the day, his skin hanging loose, as if his bones were shrinking inside him. "You shouldn't be out here, boy," Elias rasped. His voice sounded like gravel grinding together. "Just needed a break from the transmission talk," JT tried to joke, but the humor died in the cold air. "Elias, is everything... is everything okay with the season? We saw that buck today. It was acting strange." Elias’s eyes widened slightly, the whites showing in a ring of panic. He stepped closer, invading JT's personal space. The smell coming off him wasn't tobacco; it was something sour, like milk that had turned in the sun. "You didn't shoot it," Elias whispered. It wasn't a question. "Dad... he hesitated. I don't know why." Elias let out a harsh, barking laugh that was devoid of humor. "Hesitated. Yeah. That's one word for it." He looked over his shoulder at the woods, then back to JT, gripping JT’s arm with fingers that felt like iron pincers. "Listen to me. You pack up. You get in that truck and you drive south. Tonight." "What?" JT pulled back, confused. "We paid for the week. We haven't even dressed a deer yet." "There ain't no deer worth dying for," Elias hissed. "Not this time. The woods... they're hungry. It’s the moon. She’s full tomorrow night. You don't want to be here when she peaks." JT looked at the old man, trying to square the Elias he knew—the blowhard, the guide—with this scared, trembling wreck. "What are you talking about? 'Hungry'? It's just woods, Elias. It’s just animals." Elias leaned in until his face was inches from JT’s. His breath was hot and foul. "You think that buck was waiting for you? You think it wanted to die? Maybe. But what happens when the hunter stops hunting and starts... *joining*? You saw it. You know." JT felt the blood drain from his face. The shame he’d felt in the clearing curdled into cold fear. "You saw us?" "I saw the look on your daddy's face," Elias said, releasing JT’s arm and stepping back into the shadows. "I've seen that look before. On men who walked into the timber and didn't come out men. You leave before full moon, or you stay and become part of the menu. Or worse." "Worse?" JT asked, his voice barely a whisper. Elias didn't answer. He just turned and walked away into the dark, moving with a strange, shambling gait, disappearing around the side of the generator shed. JT stood alone on the porch for a long time. The silence of the woods was absolute. No crickets, no owls, no wind in the branches. Just the heavy, pressing weight of the trees watching him. He looked at the moon again. It seemed higher now, larger, its craters staring down like blind eyes. He thought about going back inside, telling Mike and his father what Elias had said. He imagined the conversation: *Hey, the guide thinks we’re going to turn into deer or get eaten by the moon, let's pack up.* They’d look at him with that same concerned, pitying look they gave him when he flinched at the thunder. They’d tell him he was tired, that the city was getting to him. And worse, a small, traitorous voice in the back of his mind whispered: *What if they don't want to go?* He remembered the way his father had looked at the buck. Not with hunger, but with *recognition*. JT turned back to the door, his hand hovering over the latch. Inside, he could hear the low murmur of the television and the clink of silverware. It sounded safe. It sounded normal. But as he stood there, looking at the reflection of the moon in the dark glass of the window, he saw his own face staring back—and for a second, just a split second, the reflection didn't move when he did. It just watched him with dark, flat eyes. JT yanked the door open and stepped inside, locking it behind him. But as the deadbolt slid home with a heavy *thunk*, he knew it didn't matter. The feeling was undeniable now, crawling up his spine like a centipede. They weren't the only ones in the lodge. And whatever was outside with the moon was starting to get inside, too.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation successfully maintains King's blend of domestic realism and creeping unease. The dinner scene grounds us in mundane detail (transmission talk as "performance"), and the Elias exchange provides the needed dialogue while escalating dread through his transformation from blowhard to terrified old man. JT's isolation is well-preserved: he can't tell his family, and the story tracks his internal rationalizations convincingly. Strengths: The imagery is mostly strong ("eyes reflecting the orange dance, looking like two hot coals embedded in leather"; the swollen moon "pressing against the fabric of the sky"). The reflection-with-flat-eyes payoff is a solid, earned beat that ties back to the buck's eyes. Pacing builds steadily toward the Elias warning and the porch climax. Weaknesses: Elias's warning is somewhat conventional horror-exposition—the Wise Old Local who knows the secret and tells the protagonist to leave is a stock trope, delivered with familiar lines ("The woods... they're hungry"). "You don't want to be here when she peaks" borders on cliché. Some tell-don't-show slips in ("shame... curdled into cold fear," "feeling a sudden, vertiginous disconnect"). A few similes overreach ("fingers that felt like iron pincers," "crawling up his spine like a centipede"—centipede is oddly specific and slightly off-tone). The "becoming part of the menu" phrasing is muddy. Minor continuity quibble: Elias was established inside at dinner, then appears outside without transition, though this could be intentional eeriness it doesn't read as such. Word count is near target. The ending lands dark, congruent with the genre and the setup. Overall this is competent, atmospheric genre fiction with a few clichéd beats and moderate reliance on familiar horror furniture, but it fulfills the prompt's requirements with reliable craft. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The alarm clock didn’t ring; it shrieked, a sound remarkably similar to a soul being unspooled from its body. Lucifer Morningstar slapped the snooze button—technically, the small, carved femur of a 14th-century heretic—and groaned into the silk pillows. He woke, as he always did, with a crick in his neck and a profound sense of bureaucratic ennui. The ceiling of his bedroom was painted with a fresco of the Fall, depicting himself in all his rebellious glory. He found it kitschy. It was like having a framed poster of your high school detention above your bed. Lucifer swung his legs out of bed. The floor was obsidian, heated to a precise seventy-two degrees. Hell was cold this time of the eon; the heating vents from the Circle of Treachary were acting up again. He shuffled to the kitchenette of his penthouse suite, which overlooked the burning sea of Gehenna. It was a prime location, excellent feng shui, though the sulfur did play havoc with his sinuses. He put the kettle on. It was a Tuesday. Or perhaps a span of time that roughly equated to the concept of a Tuesday in the mortal coil. While waiting for his tea—Earl Grey, hot, because some tropes were immutable—he checked his daily agenda. It was etched into a slate tablet by a trembling imp. * 9:00 AM: Torture Performance Review (Circle 8). * 11:00 AM: Lunch with Mammon (Discussing inflation on the price of silver). * 1:00 PM: Sign off on new punishments for fraudulent televangelists. * 3:00 PM: *She* is coming. Lucifer stared at the last item. The charcoal had been pressed harder into the stone, the jagged handwriting of the imp betraying its fear. Lilith. They were in the "off again" phase of a relationship that had lasted since the Bronze Age. The previous "on again" phase had ended three centuries ago when she had set fire to his collection of first-edition bibles during a debate about free will versus passive-aggressive silence. Since then, contact had been limited to lightning strikes, the occasional plague of locusts, and passive-aggressive notes delivered by ravens. But recently, the tenor had changed. She had been stopping by. Not to smite, not to scream, but to... linger. To sit on his velvet settee and criticize his drapes. It was terrifying. Lucifer dressed with care. He chose a three-piece suit woven from the shadows of regret, crisp and impeccable. If she was coming, he had to look like he wasn't falling apart. He had to look like the King of Damnation, not a lonely middle-manager waiting for his estranged wife to drop off the alimony checks. The day was a blur of administrative horrors. The Torture Performance Review was dull. The head imp of the Malebolge was insisting that flaying was "out" and "psychological waterboarding" was the new standard. Lucifer signed the request for more budget just to make the headache stop. Lunch with Mammon was worse. Mammon wouldn’t stop talking about cryptocurrency. "It’s digital souls, Luke!" Mammon said, shoving a forkful of pasta primavera—sauce made from reduced envy—into his mouth. "Decentralized damnation. No overhead." "Fascinating," Lucifer lied, staring at his reflection in his spoon. He looked tired. He looked like he needed a hug, or at least a really good war. By 3:00 PM, Lucifer was back in his study, pretending to read a scroll. The air pressure dropped. The temperature spiked by ten degrees. The smell of ozone and pomegranates filled the room. She didn’t knock. She simply manifested, sitting in the high-backed leather chair opposite his desk. Lilith looked devastating. She wore a dress the color of dried blood, cut on a bias that would have made a mortal queen weep with envy. Her hair was a storm cloud of dark curls, pinned back with what looked like the finger bones of a judge. "Your receptionist is a gibbering wreck," she said by way of greeting. "I had to turn him into a newt just to get some peace." "Gary," Lucifer sighed, rubbing his temples. "I just hired him. He was supposed to be resilient." "Resilience is boring," Lilith said, crossing her legs. She placed a scorched leather purse on his desk. It smelled of bonfires and retail therapy. "I came to return this." Lucifer eyed the purse. "I’ve never seen that before." "I know. I bought it in the mortal realm. 1920s. Chicago." She opened the clasp. "Look." Lucifer leaned forward. Inside the purse was a jumble of items that made no sense together. A thimble made of bone. A parking ticket from a city that no longer existed. A small, glass jar containing a single, perfectly preserved hummingbird. "Trinkets," she said softly. "I find them on the surface. Humans leave the most interesting things behind when they... move on." "It's clutter, Lilith," Lucifer said, though his voice lacked its usual bite. He reached out and touched the thimble. It was cold. "Why are you showing me this?" "Because I thought you’d like the hummingbird," she said, defensive. "It’s iridescent." "It’s dead, Lili." "It’s preserved," she corrected sharply. The old spark flared in her eyes—the dangerous, beautiful madness that had made him fall for her in the first place. "Not everything has to be about fire and screaming, Lucifer. Sometimes it’s just about... keeping things." She snapped the purse shut. The silence that followed was heavy, filled with the weight of ten thousand years of arguments and make-up sex and apocalyptic threats. Lucifer looked at her, really looked at her. She wasn't here to gloat. She was here because the mortal realm was vast and empty, and Hell was crowded but lonely, and they were the only two beings in existence who truly remembered what the stars looked like before they were named. "Stay for dinner," Lucifer said. It wasn't a question, but it wasn't quite an order either. Lilith arched an eyebrow. "I have a coven meeting in the swamp of despair at seven." "CANCEL it," Lucifer said, his voice dropping, the echoes of the Serpent creeping in. "I have a bottle of Châteauneuf-du-Pape from a vintage I stole right before the French Revolution. I’m not drinking it alone." Lilith looked at him, her expression unreadable. She tapped her fingernails on the scorched leather of the purse. *Tap, tap, tap.* "Fine," she said, standing up. She smoothed her dress. "But if you talk about work, I’m leaving. And I’m taking the hummingbird." "It’s a deal," Lucifer said, standing as well. She walked past him, her scent lingering in the air like a bruise. She paused at the door, looking back over her shoulder. "You look tired, Lucifer," she said, her voice losing its edge, becoming something dangerously close to tender. "You should sleep. The screaming will still be there tomorrow." "I know," he said. "That’s the problem." She left the room, leaving the door open a crack. Lucifer sat back down in his chair and looked at the purse she had left on the desk. He opened it again and looked at the dead hummingbird, glittering in the dim light of the study. He poured himself a glass of the wine. It was excellent. He swirled the dark red liquid, watching the legs of the wine drip down the glass like blood on a wall. Hell was other people, yes. But sometimes, just sometimes, it was the people you couldn't live without, even when you wanted to kill them. Lucifer took a sip and waited for dinner, feeling significantly less alone, and significantly more doomed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of dark domestic comedy that largely delivers on the prompt's brief. The story successfully merges the mundane (alarm clocks, tea, lunch meetings, agendas) with the infernal (femur snooze buttons, torture performance reviews, Mammon discussing cryptocurrency as "decentralized damnation"). The Gaiman influence is evident in the wry, understated narration and the melancholy beneath the comedy. Strengths: The opening is strong—the shrieking alarm, the kitschy fresco of the Fall compared to "a framed poster of your high school detention above your bed" is a genuinely funny, precise image. The bureaucratic ennui is well-drawn. Lilith's purse of trinkets—the bone thimble, the parking ticket from a city that no longer exists, the preserved hummingbird—is an excellent device, showing her character through objects and giving the story its emotional core. The hummingbird exchange ("It's dead, Lili." / "It's preserved") is the best dialogue in the piece, economical and revealing. The ending wisely avoids a full reconciliation; the "on again" turn is signaled but not consummated, which feels earned and appropriately tentative. The final line's "significantly less alone, and significantly more doomed" lands well. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally reaches for easy jokes (Gary the receptionist turned into a newt is a Monty Python borrow; "Earl Grey, hot" is a Picard reference that feels like a wink rather than a joke). Some descriptions lean on cliché: Lilith "looked devastating," her dress "the color of dried blood," "storm cloud of dark curls"—serviceable but predictable. The middle section (Mammon lunch, torture review) is efficient but a bit list-like, and the emotional pivot, while well-motivated by the purse scene, is slightly accelerated; the "really looked at her" moment tells us the shift rather than fully dramatizing it. The line "they were the only two beings in existence who truly remembered what the stars looked like before they were named" is lovely but borders on the sentimental. The Sartre title-pun resolution ("Hell was other people, yes. But sometimes...") is a bit neat. Prose is clean and flows well, with only occasional overreach ("her scent lingering in the air like a bruise" works; "the weight of ten thousand years of arguments and make-up sex and apocalyptic threats" is a good comic beat). Overall, this is skilled, polished work with genuine wit and emotional resonance, held back from excellence by a few stock images and a slightly rushed emotional turn. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 74.1
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
The air in the *ludus* never truly circulated. It hung heavy, a stagnant soup of sweat, sawdust, and the sharp, metallic tang of the olive oil we rubbed into our skin after training. It was a smell that lived in the pores, one no amount of scraping with the *strigil* could ever fully remove. I woke to the vibration of the stone floor beneath my straw pallet. The morning bell hadn’t rung yet, but the city above was already stirring. Rome is a beast that never sleeps; it merely snores through the watches of the night and wakes ravenous. I sat up, the wool blanket scratching at the scars mapping my torso. My cellmate, Diodorus, a Thracian with a broken nose and a disposition to match, was already awake. He was staring at the ceiling, his chest rising and falling in a rhythm too controlled to be natural. “Today,” he whispered, the word sounding like a stone dropping into a well. “The Emperor is in the box.” I didn’t answer. I didn’t need to. We all knew what that meant. Commodus wasn’t a man who appreciated a clean, technical bout. He wanted blood, he wanted drama, and he wanted to play the part of the divine Hercules. If the fight dragged on too long, he might just decide to clear the floor of everyone, winner and loser alike, just to see something new. I swung my legs over the edge of the bed. The cold bit at my heels. This was the height of the empire, they said. The marble was polished, the aqueducts flowed with sweet water, and the legions kept the barbarians at the gate. But down here in the underbelly, we were just the lubricant for the gears of the machine. We were the *munus*, the duty owed to the dead, a sacrifice to keep the mob pacified with bread and circuses so they wouldn’t notice the rot eating away at the Senate’s foundations. I stood and walked to the small, barred window near the ceiling. Outside, I could hear the low, distant hum of the Flavian Amphitheatre. It sounded like the ocean, but angrier. Fifty, maybe sixty thousand souls gathering to watch us die. The political climate was tense; the grain dole had been late last week, and the whispers of conspiracy against the Emperor were thick enough to choke on. Today was a distraction, a necessary spectacle to buy Commodus another week of adoration. A guard clanged his spear against the iron bars of our cell door. “Gruel,” he grunted, shoving a wooden bowl through the slot. It was barley, watered down and lukewarm. I ate it mechanically. It was fuel, nothing more. Then came the ritual. I reached into the small hollowed-out space beneath the stone bench where I kept my private things. A smooth river stone, black as obsidian, and a small pouch of dried sage. Before every fight, while the others sharpened their blades and checked their *manicae*—the leather arm guards—I performed my rite. I placed the stone on the floor and sat cross-legged before it. Closing my eyes, I inhaled the scent of the sage as I crushed it between my fingers. It was a sharp, green smell that cut through the stench of the prison. I whispered a prayer not to Mars, the god of war, for Mars was fickle and loved only slaughter. I prayed to Mania, the goddess of the dead, asking her to keep her gates closed to me for one more afternoon. I rubbed the sage dust onto the soles of my feet, a superstition from my childhood in Gaul, believing it would keep me grounded to the living earth. “What good is dust against a *secutor*’s sword?” Diodorus scoffed, lacing up his sandals. “It keeps the shadows at bay,” I muttered, returning the stone to its hiding place. We were marched out to the armory. The sunlight hit us like a physical blow, blinding after the dimness of the cells. The armorer, a one-eyed Greek named Nikias, handed me my gear. I was a *murmillo*, the fish-man. I took the heavy, rectangular shield, the rim bitten and dented from previous bouts. I strapped on the bronze greaves, the metal cold against my calves. Finally, the helmet. It was the worst part. The moment the helmet came down, the world narrowed to a slit. The sounds of the armory—the clanking of iron, the cursing of the men, the barking of the *lanista*—became muffled, distant. I became a metal creature, less human, more instrument. The *lanista*, a man named Quintus who bought us like cattle and sold our deaths like tickets, walked the line. He looked nervous. He had a lot of coin riding on the afternoon’s main event, and with Commodus watching, the stakes were higher than gold. “Remember,” Quintus said, his voice tight. “The crowd decides your fate. If you go down, stay down. Don’t beg, and don’t thrash. Die with dignity, and they might spare you. Disappoint them, and you’ll wish you had died in the sand.” He paused in front of me. “And you, Crixus. The Emperor wants to see the new style from the East. Don’t just hack. Give him a show.” I nodded, the leather strap of the helmet digging into my chin. We began the march. The tunnel leading up to the arena floor was sloped upward, a ramp toward the light. The air grew hotter as we ascended, carrying the smell of the arena itself—that distinct, coppery scent of old blood baking in the sun, mixed with the dust of the *harena* and the roasting meat sold to the spectators. The roar of the crowd changed. It wasn't just a hum anymore; it was a physical pressure, vibrating in my chest and rattling my teeth. It was the sound of Rome at its apex and its nadir, a thousand throats screaming for entertainment, for justice, for blood. We stepped out of the gloom of the hypogeum and into the blinding white light of the arena. The sight always stole the breath, no matter how many times I saw it. The tiered seating rose up like a mountain range of white marble, a sea of colorful togas and shifting faces. The awning, the *velarium*, was unfurled, casting giant, striped shadows across the sand. High above, in the imperial box, I could see the purple. I couldn’t see his face, but I felt his gaze. It was a heavy, suffocating thing. I took my position. The sand shifted beneath my sandals, warm and loose. I raised my shield, the weight familiar and comforting on my arm. Across the arena, the gate lifted, and my opponent stepped out. A *retiarius*, a net-man. He danced lightly, his trident flashing in the sun, a stark contrast to my heavy, plodding infantry style. The crowd’s roar swelled, crashing over us like a wave. The ground trembled slightly, not from an earthquake, but from the collective stomping of sixty thousand feet. I stood still, waiting. I touched the spot on my ankle where the sage dust lay, feeling the grit against my skin. I thought of the grain ships docking at Ostia, the senators counting their coins, the Emperor playing his games. I was a pawn in their politics, a actor in their tragedy. But for this moment, standing in the center of the ring, the only thing that mattered was the sun on my back and the man with the net. The world narrowed down to the slit in my helmet. The noise faded into a dull thrum. I took a deep breath, tasting the dust and the iron. “Hail, Emperor, we who are about to die salute you,” I mouthed, the words silent inside the metal shell. Then, I lowered my center of gravity and waited for the net to fly.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a competent, atmospheric slice-of-life piece that hits most of the prompt's requirements: first person, past tense, roughly 1000 words, non-combat (it ends at the threshold of a fight without depicting it), rich sensory detail, and clear gestures toward Roman politics (Commodus, grain dole, conspiracy whispers, "bread and circuses"). Strengths: The sensory palette is the piece's best asset—the stagnant air of the ludus, the sage ritual, the coppery smell of old blood baking in the sand, the roar as physical pressure. The narrator's private superstition (praying to Mania rather than Mars) is a genuinely good characterizing detail, and the exchange with Diodorus about it is the strongest dialogue moment. The political framing—gladiators as "lubricant for the gears," spectacle as a distraction from Senate rot—is efficiently woven in without lecturing. Weaknesses: The piece leans on well-worn gladiator-fiction furniture: the lanista's "die with dignity" speech, the "we who are about to die" line, the fish-man vs. net-man pairing, the name Crixus (borrowed wholesale from Spartacus), Commodus as the theatrical mad emperor. These are all genre staples, and the piece does little to subvert or freshen them. The prose occasionally strains—"a stone dropping into a well," "a beast that never sleeps... snores"—and there's a typo ("a actor"). Some telling creeps in ("He was nervous," "The political climate was tense"). The ending is effective but predictable: the narrowing of the world to the helmet slit is a familiar beat. The emotional range is somewhat narrow—dread and fatalism, well rendered, but little surprise or interiority beyond resignation. Diodorus and Quintus are functional sketches rather than people. Overall: solid professional-grade historical fiction that fulfills the brief with craft, but not inventive enough to feel like more than a well-executed exercise in a familiar genre. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**15th October 1963** **The Northern Lighthouse Board, Provisional Posting** **Skerryvore Rock (via Oban)** Dear Mam, I’m writing this before the post boat leaves, so I’ll make it quick. The rock is wet, even when it’s no raining. The sea spray grabs hold of everything. It’s a good job, though. The money is better than the docks, and the Board gave me a new set of oilskins. The tower itself is a grand thing. Brick and granite, tall as a kirk steeple. My feet are still finding their land legs after the crossing. The keeper here, a man named McTavish, says the wind sings songs if you listen long enough. I think he’s just trying to scare the new boy. The work is heavy. We have to haul the oil up the stairs, three flights, in big brass cans. My shoulders are screaming, but it’s honest sweat. Tell Da I’m not drinking the wages. I’ll send a postal order next week. Your son, Ewan *** **22nd October 1963** **14 Tenement Street** **Glasgow** Dearest Ewan, It was good to get your scribble. I’ve pinned it to the board by the kettle. Your Da says to tell you that oilskins don’t keep the cold out of your bones, so wear the wool vest I packed for you, even if you think it looks thick. Don’t mind Mr. McTavish and his songs. You’ve always had a good head on your shoulders, Ewan. Just keep it down and do the work. The rent is paid up to November, so don’t you fret about the house. We are fine. Mrs. Higgins next door asked after you. She says you’re too young to be stuck on a rock in the middle of God’s nowhere. I told her a man has to go where the work is. Come home safe. Love, Mam *** **2nd January 1964** **Skerryvore Rock** Mam, Happy New Year to you and Da. McTavish went off on the relief boat yesterday. They moved him to a station on the mainland. It’s just me and the new assistant, a quiet lad from Lewis named Murdo. We don’t talk much. The wind is too loud for chatting anyway. It’s the dark that gets you. In Glasgow, you’ve got the streetlamps and the glow from the factory windows. Here, when the lamp is doused in the morning, it’s black. You have to watch your hands to make sure they’re still yours. I’ve started a tally on the wall of the storeroom. Marks for the ships that pass. One hundred and twelve since October. Sometimes I wave, even though I know they can’t see me. It makes me feel less like a ghost. Keep the fire lit for me, Ewan *** **15th March 1964** **Glasgow** Ewan, Your letters are getting shorter. Is everything alright? You didn’t mention the money in the last one, not that I’m asking. I’m just worried. Da had a bad turn with his chest last week. He’s sitting up now, drinking the tea you sent. He says the salt air is doing you good, but I hear a shake in your words, Ewan. Are you eating? Murdo the Lewis man—does he pull his weight? If it’s too much, there’s work at the shipyard again. They’re taking men back on. Don’t be proud. Come home. Love, Mam *** **10th April 1964** **Skerryvore Rock** Mam, Don’t be daft. I’m not coming back with my tail between my legs. The shipyard is closed to me. I have a position here. It’s hard, aye. The clockwork mechanism is a beast. You have to wind it every hour and twenty minutes. It takes ten minutes of solid cranking, heavy enough to make your teeth grind. If you miss a rotation, the weights drop, the lamp stops, and some trawler smashes onto the rocks. That’s the weight of it, Mam. It sits on your chest even when you’re off watch. Last night, a gale hit us. The tower was shaking like a dog in a thunderstorm. The glass was rattling in the frames. I lay in my bunk listening to the waves hitting the stone below, thinking about how much water was between us. Murdo just slept through it. I don’t know how he does it. I’m fine. Truly. Just tired. Ewan *** **Telegram** **14th November 1964** **From: Northern Lighthouse Board, Oban** **To: Mrs. B. MacInnes, 14 Tenement Street, Glasgow** STOP. SUPPLY BOAT UNABLE TO DOCK SKERRYVORE DUE TO WEATHER STOP. PROVISIONS LOW BUT KEEPERS SAFE STOP. RELIEF DELAYED INDEFINITELY STOP. WILL ADVISE STOP. *** **20th November 1964** **Skerryvore Rock** Mam, I’m writing this on the back of an old logbook because we’re out of paper. The boat hasn’t made it for three weeks. We ran out of fresh food a week ago. It’s tinned peas and hard biscuits now. The coal bunker is damp, and the smoke won’t draw right in the kitchen. We’re sitting in our coats to eat. But that’s no the worst of it. The main bearing in the rotation gear seized up two nights ago. It was during the storm. The noise was like a train crash. I tried to grease it, but the metal was hot enough to burn the skin off my palm. I had to take a hammer to it to free the jam. I was up on the gallery for four hours, Mam. The waves were coming right over the railing, freezing solid the second they hit the glass. I was hanging onto the rail with one hand, swinging the hammer with the other, thinking if I slip, I’m gone. No one would even find the body. I got it turning again. The light didn’t go out. But looking down at the black water, spinning round and round... I felt like I wanted to let go. Not to die, just to stop the spinning. Murdo found me on the floor of the lantern room this morning. I must have fallen asleep there. He didn’t say a word. Just made tea. I’m scared, Mam. Not of the sea. I’m scared of the quiet in my own head. Ewan *** **Telegram** **22nd November 1964** **From: Mrs. B. MacInnes** **To: Ewan MacInnes, Skerryvore Rock** COMING HOME DO NOT ARGUE DA BORROWED CAR. *** **15th December 1964** **Oban** Dear Mam, I’m sitting in a café in Oban. The relief boat finally got in this morning. I felt sick leaving the rock. I kept looking back, thinking the light would go out the second I stepped off the granite. I’ve resigned. The Superintendent tried to talk me round, offered me a transfer to a shore station, but I couldn’t sign the paper. My hand was shaking too bad. I’m not coming back to the shipyard, though. Da wrote and told me about the garage in town needing a mechanic. I think I’d like to work with engines that don’t have the weight of men’s lives on them. I saw a tree today. A real one, growing out of the pavement. I stood and looked at it for ten minutes. People were staring, but I didn’t care. It was just brown and bare, but it was the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen. I’ll be on the train tonight. Don’t wait up. I just want to walk the streets and hear the noise of the city. Love, Ewan
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative succeeds on most of its own terms. The correspondence format is handled well: letters, telegrams, and dates create a convincing arc over fourteen months. The two voices are distinct—Ewan's clipped, practical Scots-inflected prose versus his mother's fussing, love-disguised-as-logistics tone. The mother's line "COMING HOME DO NOT ARGUE DA BORROWED CAR" is a genuine highlight: the terse telegram form becomes a moment of maternal force and dark comedy at once. The plot unfolds believably through the letters: initial bravado, erosion of morale in the dark months, father's illness as counterweight, the supply failure, the mechanical crisis, and the psychological break. The detail work is strong—the clockwork wound every hour and twenty minutes, the tally of ships on the storeroom wall, waving at ships that can't see him, the frozen spray on the lantern glass. These earn the story's emotional weight. The climactic letter ("I'm scared... of the quiet in my own head") is the strongest passage, and Murdo's wordless tea-making is a fine show-don't-touch moment. Weaknesses: the resolution arrives somewhat quickly—the final letter ties everything off in a tidy, slightly too convenient paragraph (resignation, new job waiting, no real cost). The tree-in-Oban epiphany gestures toward sentimentality and borders on a cliché of "restored appreciation of ordinary life," though the specificity ("brown and bare") mostly saves it. The father's chest illness is raised and dropped without consequence. McTavish's "wind sings songs" line is a bit of stock foreshadowing. Minor anachronism risk in the postal order details but these are fine. Some phrasing ("honest sweat," "weight of men's lives") edges toward the familiar. The pacing is tight rather than meandering, and prose is clean, restrained, appropriately plain for working-class voices—no purple excess. Overall a skilled, controlled piece with an authentic emotional trajectory, slightly hampered by a rushed and overly neat ending. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 57.8
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The ambient noise of the bistro is sitting at a steady 65 decibels, a comfortable hum, but the acoustic dampening panels on the ceiling are installed with a slight gap near the north corner. A potential ingress point for sound leakage, or perhaps a structural weakness in the drywall. I force my eyes to stop tracing the seam and focus back on Maya. She is smiling. The smile is genuine—crinkles around the eyes, symmetrical lip elevation. No signs of social engineering or deceit. She is authentic. This is good. This is what I wanted. A human connection. But my brain is still running a background daemon on the waiter’s POS system. It looked like a legacy Square reader, likely running an outdated Android kernel. If I wanted to, I could probably bump his network with a malicious QR code, but I won’t. I’m reformed. I’m a White Hat. I protect systems now. I protect people. "So, yeah," Maya is saying, gesturing with her fork. "I stopped playing Standard years ago. Too much churn. I’m all about Commander now." Commander. A multiplayer format. High chaos variance. This aligns with her personality type—she’s adaptive, social, enjoys complex interactions. "I built a *Krenko, Mob Boss* deck recently," she says. "Just goblins. Pure aggro." *Krenko*. Token generation. Exponential growth. She values speed and overwhelming force. A "swarm the board" mentality. She doesn't go for subtle, surgical strikes; she prefers brute force denial-of-service attacks on life totals. I nod, trying to look engaged in a romantic way, not an analytical way. "That sounds... chaotic." "It is! But sometimes I switch to *Muldrotha, the Gravetide* for value." *Muldrotha*. Graveyard recursion. Persistent threats. She likes redundancy. If a plan fails, she has a backup ready to deploy from the discard pile. Resilience. A desirable trait in a partner. I file this away: *Subject prefers redundancy over fragile glass-cannon strategies.* "But honestly," she laughs, "I have a soft spot for *Counterspell*." Control. Of course. *Counterspell* represents total interaction. Denial of the opponent’s agency. She likes to be in charge of the stack. She wants to dictate the flow of the game. She’s dominant but playful. The appetizer arrives. Calamari. I watch her pick up a ring. She dips it. Good motor control. "I also run *Sol Ring* in every deck," she adds. "Obviously." *Sol Ring*. Fast mana. Acceleration. She’s impatient. She wants to reach the endgame before anyone else. She’s willing to take risks—*Sol Ring* is a target; playing it paints a bullseye on your back. She accepts the threat of being focused in exchange for early advantage. High risk, high reward. Just like agreeing to a first date with a guy she met on a subreddit dedicated to vintage tech. This is going well. The data points are converging on a profile of someone who is intelligent, strategic, and perhaps a bit competitive. I feel a flush of dopamine. This is "chemistry," I assume. Then, the phone buzzes. It’s on the table, face down, vibrating against the wood. It’s a mid-range Android, maybe two years old. The screen lights up with a notification. "Sorry," Maya says. "I should check this. My sister is having a crisis." She reaches for the device. I watch. I can’t help it. It’s instinctual. Her hand hovers. She swipes up from the bottom edge to engage the lock screen. Then, she enters her pattern. My eyes lock onto her finger movement. It starts at the top left node. Diagonal down to the bottom right. Then horizontal all the way to the left. Then diagonal up to the top right. A 'Z'. She drew a 'Z'. I feel a physical twitch in my left temple. A 'Z'? On a 3x3 grid? That is four nodes. The entropy is laughable. That is a pattern a toddler could guess. That is a pattern that has a 1 in 9 chance of being guessed on the first try if you assume the user starts in a corner. The smudge trails on the screen are probably visible under a UV light; she’s essentially broadcasting her credentials to anyone with a flashlight and a grudge. She unlocks it and starts typing a reply. I try to listen to her talking about her sister’s breakup, I really do, but the vulnerability is screaming at me. It’s a critical zero-day in my evening’s operating system. How can I trust this person with my heart—metaphorically speaking—when they secure their digital life with the first letter of the alphabet? It’s negligence. It’s asking to be socially engineered. If I were a black hat, I’d have her identity stolen, her crypto drained, and her smart toaster turned against her before the main course arrived. The silence stretches. She puts the phone down, screen black. "Everything okay?" I ask. My voice sounds tight. Strained. "Yeah, just drama." She smiles, taking a sip of her wine. I should let it go. I should pivot back to Magic. Ask her about *Swords to Plowshares*. Ask her if she prefers aggro or control. But the exploit is right there. It’s an open port. I have to patch it. I have to make her secure. "So," I say, casual as a rootkit, "that pattern." "What pattern?" She looks confused. "The unlock pattern. On your phone." "Oh." She laughs, a little nervous. "Yeah, it’s just a Z. Easy to remember." "Too easy," I say. The words are out before I can run a heuristic check on their social impact. "That’s a four-point pattern. If you factor in the oily residue on your screen, a threat actor could deduce that with a 98% confidence interval in under five seconds. You’re effectively transmitting your password in cleartext every time you check the weather." The silence that falls over the table is heavier than the previous silence. This isn't companionable silence; this is a kernel panic. She blinks. "I... what?" "It’s a massive security vulnerability," I press on, unable to abort the script. "You need at least six nodes. Random non-adjacent. Preferably biometrics, though fingerprint sensors on that model are spoofable with high-res gelatin prints. But seriously, a 'Z'? You might as well use '1234'." She puts her wine glass down. Hard. The stem wobbles. "I'm sorry," she says, her voice dropping an octave. "Are you critiquing my password security on a first date?" "I'm just saying," I backpedal, realizing the stack trace is leading to a crash, "it’s for your own protection. I notice these things. It’s my job. It’s how my brain works. I see a system, I see the flaws. I don't want you to get... hacked." "I’m not a server, David," she says. "I’m a girl eating calamari." "I know that. But social engineering is the primary vector for identity theft. If someone swipes that phone—" "Who is going to swipe my phone?" She’s looking at me now like I’m the malware. "We’re in a tapas place." "It doesn't matter. Threat modeling is about preparation, not just immediate danger." I’m digging. Why am I digging? I should stop digging. The hole is deep enough to bury the relationship. "Look, just... change the pattern. Maybe an 'M' or something complex. Or use a passphrase. A diceware passphrase." She stares at me. The *Muldrotha* resilience is gone. The *Krenko* aggression is rising. I can see it in her eyes. She’s assessing *me* now. I am the vulnerability. "You know," she says slowly, "I was really enjoying talking about Magic. I felt like we had a connection." "We do," I insist. "I cataloged your card choices. You like value engines and recursion. You’re smart." "But you couldn't turn off the hacker mode for five minutes to just... exist?" "I exist," I say weakly. "I just exist securely." She picks up her napkin, drops it on the table. The signal termination. The connection is closing. "I think I’m going to head out," she says. "My sister needs me anyway." "She texted you twenty minutes ago," I point out, because accuracy is a curse. "Right." She stands up. "Well. It was... educational." I watch her leave. I watch her walk toward the door. I check the exit path. She’s moving toward the street. No physical barriers. I sit back in the chair. The waiter comes by. "How was everything, sir? Can I get you the check?" "Fine," I say. "The check is fine." I look at the empty seat. I replay the incident. The exploit was the phone. The payload was my critique. The result was a total system failure. I reach into my pocket and pull out my own phone. It’s locked, of course. 12-character alphanumeric with special symbols, 2FA enabled, hardware key required for pairing. I stare at the black screen. I catalog the evening's data: * Target: Maya. * Strategy: Aggro-Control. * Vulnerability: Trust. * Result: Patch rejected. I unlock my phone using a randomized, 8-node pattern that looks like a Jackson Pollock painting. I open the notes app. I delete the draft text that said *Second Date Ideas*. I order a scotch. I scan the room for other vulnerabilities. The couple in the corner is speaking too loudly about their investments. The bartender is using the same rag for the glass rims and the counter surface. Cross-contamination risk. I take a sip of the scotch. It burns. It’s a good burn. It’s authentic. I really liked her *Muldrotha* deck, too.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a strong execution of the prompt's core concept: a reformed hacker whose threat-modeling brain cannot stop analyzing everything, including his date. The internal monologue voice is consistent and effective—clinical, taxonomic, translating human behavior into security terminology. The Magic: The Gathering profiling device is clever, using real cards (Krenko, Muldrotha, Sol Ring, Counterspell) as personality diagnostics, which both satisfies the fandom requirement and characterizes the protagonist's inability to experience anything without parsing it. The phone pattern incident lands well. The 'Z' pattern observation is plausible and the protagonist's inability to stop himself ("casual as a rootkit," "unable to abort the script") is the emotional crux. The dialogue during the confrontation is the strongest section—Maya's "I'm not a server, David. I'm a girl eating calamari" is a genuinely good line, and her escalating frustration feels earned. Weaknesses: The piece leans heavily on a single joke (security metaphor applied to everything), and while the format sustains it, some entries are filler rather than insight ("Good motor control" while watching her eat calamari is funny but thin). The ending's "catalog the evening's data" list is a bit tidy and self-congratulatory in its cleverness. The final beat—scanning the room for new vulnerabilities and the wistful Muldrotha callback—works, though the "It's a good burn. It's authentic" line flirts with sentimentality. Maya herself is thinly characterized beyond her card choices; she exists mostly as a surface for the protagonist's projections, though arguably that's the point. Some technical flourishes ("98% confidence interval") are intentionally absurd but occasionally read as the author showing off rather than the character. The prose is functional rather than elegant—short declarative sentences suit the voice, but there's little musicality. Overall: a competent, entertaining, well-structured piece that fully satisfies the prompt with wit and a satisfying arc, without elevating itself beyond its conceit.
